explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God said, “They are surely My people, sons who will not be disloyal.” Then the verse says, “So He became their Savior.” The next verse tells us how He did it: “In His love and compassion He redeemed them.” That's a whole lot of rescuing.

I get the guess, because the prayer does get to some hard moments later on. But this verse is about what God became after He called them His people. The text says, “So He became their Savior.” Judge isn't the word here.

Teacher sounds cozy, like a cookie class with name tags. But that's not the word in the verse. After God said, “They are surely My people,” the text says, “So He became their Savior.” Rescuing is the job here.

I understand the guess. We've all had a friend who gets real quiet when things go wrong. But that's not what the text says here. It says, “In all their distress, He too was afflicted.” God didn't stand off to the side. He was in it with them.

That's right, it's false. The prayer says, “In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them.” He didn't keep His distance. He was hurting right along with them. Friend, that is a close God.

Right. The prayer says Israel “rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit. So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them.” I think that's one of the heaviest lines in the whole prayer. It's good to know it's in there, because the prayer doesn't hide it.

Master is a close-sounding word, but it isn't the one in the verse. The text says, “So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them.” That's a heavy turn, and the prayer says it plainly. I think that's why the questions pour out right after.

Stranger would mean He just walked off, but that's not what the text says. It says, “So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them.” That's a heavier word than stranger. It's a hard line, and the prayer doesn't soften it.

Yes, the sea. The people remember and ask, “Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock?” They're looking back at the days of Moses, Israel's leader. A few verses later it says He “divided the waters before them.” You don't forget a walk like that.

Good river, but it isn't the one in this verse. The question says, “Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock?” The prayer goes on to say He “divided the waters before them.” So the sea is the answer.

Mountains do show up in this prayer, but later. They quake at God's presence in Isaiah 64:1. Here the verse asks, “Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock?” The answer is sea.

explanations.answer: To make His name famous forever
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The prayer says He “divided the waters before them to gain for Himself everlasting renown.” Renown means a name people know. And a name known forever is a pretty big batch of fame.

explanations.answer: To show Moses was worth following
explanations.explanation: Moses is in the verse, since God's arm led them “by the right hand of Moses.” But the reason the prayer gives is different. He divided the waters “to gain for Himself everlasting renown.” The text doesn't say it was to prove anything about Moses.

explanations.answer: To teach His people to obey Him
explanations.explanation: Obedience is a good lesson, but this verse doesn't give it as the reason. The prayer says He divided the waters “to gain for Himself everlasting renown.” Verse 14 says something similar, that He led His people this way “to make for Yourself a glorious name.” So the reason is His name.

Close, but the verse says the opposite at the end. He led them “through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble.” Picture a horse trotting along steady, no wobbles. I couldn't walk across my own counter that smoothly.

Right, it's false. The verse says He led them “through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble.” No stumbling at all. A horse in open country doesn't trip, and neither did they.

That's it. The prayer says, “Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained.” Notice the one praying isn't pretending everything is fine. They say how it feels and ask God to look down and see. I think honest prayers like that are the best kind.

That's the opposite of what the prayer says. It asks, “Where are Your zeal and might?” Then it says, “Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained.” The one praying feels that compassion is being held back.

explanations.answer: It was given to the enemies
explanations.explanation: The prayer never says that. It says, “Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained.” That means held back, and it says nothing about being handed to anyone else. Enemies come up later in the prayer, but not as getting God's compassion.

Yes, Father. “Yet You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us.” Then it says it again: “You, O LORD, are our Father.” Even with the family tree turning away, the prayer holds on to that name.

King is a grand title, but it isn't the one this prayer reaches for. The verse says, “You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name.” The prayer says Father twice in that one verse. It must be an important word.

Rock is a sturdy name, but it isn't in this verse. The prayer says, “You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name.” Father comes right after the line about Abraham and Israel not knowing them. So that's the name they hold on to.
Yes. The prayer says, “Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage.” That comes right after the hard questions. They don't just ask why. They ask Him to come back.

That's not in the verse. After the questions, the prayer says, “Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage.” The ask is for God Himself to come back. No new leader is mentioned.

Enemies do come up in the next verse, trampling the sanctuary. But the ask in this verse is different. The prayer says, “Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage.” They want God to come back to them.

That's right. The prayer says, “For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place, but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary.” A short while, then the trampling. I think this part is a hard thing to say out loud, and the prayer says it anyway.
The verse says it is true. The prayer says, “For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place.” Then it adds, “but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary.” It was only a short while.

Yes. The prayer asks God to come down “to make Your name known to Your enemies, so that the nations will tremble at Your presence!” The picture is fire making water boil. Water that's been sitting calm starts bubbling, and everybody notices.

Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. It says the prayer asks God to come down “to make Your name known to Your enemies, so that the nations will tremble at Your presence!” The prayer is looking outward, at enemies and nations.

No kings in this verse, friend. The prayer wants God to come down “to make Your name known to Your enemies.” After that it says, “so that the nations will tremble at Your presence!” The ones who need to learn His name are the enemies.

That's right. The prayer says, “From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him.” Nobody ever heard of another God like that, never mind saw one. And the LORD acts for those who wait.

The verse says it is true. It reads, “From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him.” So no one has seen any other God. This one is the One who acts for those who wait.

explanations.answer: How they can be saved if they stay in their sins
explanations.explanation: Yes. Right after “Surely You were angry, for we sinned,” the prayer asks, “How can we be saved if we remain in our sins?” They don't make excuses. They just ask the honest question.

explanations.answer: Why He ever chose them to be His people
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the prayer. After admitting they sinned, it asks, “How can we be saved if we remain in our sins?” This is a prayer about needing rescue. It doesn't question why they were chosen.

explanations.answer: When their enemies will finally leave the land
explanations.explanation: The prayer doesn't ask that here. Right after saying they sinned, it asks, “How can we be saved if we remain in our sins?” The question is about their own sin. They're not pointing at anyone else yet.

The verse says the opposite. The prayer says, “Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags.” Filthy rags would not clean up anything. They can't make up for sin.
Right, it's false. The prayer says, “all our righteous acts are like filthy rags.” It also says, “Each of us has become like something unclean.” Nothing they did could make up for their sin.

That's what the prayer says. “No one calls on Your name or strives to take hold of You. For You have hidden Your face from us and delivered us into the hand of our iniquity.” It's a sad verse, and I think it's meant to be. They say it plainly.

That's the opposite of what the verse says. The prayer says, “You have hidden Your face from us and delivered us into the hand of our iniquity.” Hidden, not shining. That's why the prayer pleads so hard.

That isn't in the verse. It says, “You have hidden Your face from us and delivered us into the hand of our iniquity.” Hidden is the word. And the very next verse starts with “But now,” and that's where it turns.

Yes, potter. “We are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand.” I'm a stamper, so I know a little about pressing shapes into soft stuff. But a potter's hands shape the whole thing, and that's the picture here.

Builder is a good job, but it isn't the picture in this verse. It says, “We are the clay, and You are the potter.” Clay goes with a potter, like dough goes with my stamper. And then comes the line, “we are all the work of Your hand.”

Farmers have their own pictures in Scripture, but not this one. Here the verse says, “We are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand.” Clay is shaped by hands. The potter is the answer.

Yes. The prayer says, “Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever.” Iniquity means sin. They name it and ask for mercy, and they don't hide it in the back of a drawer.

Names are in the prayer, but not in this plea. The verse says, “Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever.” They aren't asking to be forgotten. They're asking that their sin not be remembered forever.
The verse doesn't mention promises. It says, “Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever.” What they ask Him not to remember is their iniquity. The word means sin.

Yes. The prayer says, “Our holy and beautiful temple, where our fathers praised You, has been burned with fire, and all that was dear to us lies in ruins.” I think this one hurts. It's a hard line, and the prayer says it plainly.

explanations.answer: It was washed away in a flood
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says the temple “has been burned with fire.” I think this is a heavy line. It's good to get the details right.

explanations.answer: It was taken apart and moved
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says. The prayer says, “Our holy and beautiful temple, where our fathers praised You, has been burned with fire, and all that was dear to us lies in ruins.” I think this is a painful verse, so it's good to get it right.

That's right. The prayer ends with questions: “After all this, O LORD, will You restrain Yourself? Will You keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?” It doesn't wrap up neat. It ends with the people still asking God directly.
The verse says it is true. The very last line is, “Will You keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?” The prayer ends on a question. They are still talking to God.
